title: Malachi 4:1–6
context: The LORD of Armies continues, declaring that “the day comes, burning like a furnace,” when the proud and the wicked will be like stubble, while for those who fear his name “shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings.” He calls the people to remember the law of Moses given at Horeb and promises, “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the LORD comes,” who will turn the hearts of fathers and children to one another. Versification: English 4:1–6 is Hebrew 3:19–24; this page keeps the WEB numbers. The Gospels connect Elijah with John the Baptist (Matt 11:14; 17:11–13; Luke 1:17), while John himself says he is not Elijah (John 1:21), and readers in both traditions name these passages without merging them, reading the close of the book as shared ground about judgment, healing, and the LORD’s call to remember his word.

verses.text: “For behold, the day comes, burning like a furnace, when all the proud and all who work wickedness will be stubble. The day that comes will burn them up,” says the LORD of Armies, “so that it will leave them neither root nor branch.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For behold, the day comes, burning like a furnace, when all the proud and all who work wickedness will be stubble.” Arminian readers note the vivid image of judgment.

It answers the complaint that the proud prosper (3:15).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the certainty of God’s judgment on persistent wickedness.

Shared ground: both traditions read the furnace imagery soberly as a picture of final reckoning, leaving “neither root nor branch,” without dwelling on it.

verses.text: But to you who fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings. You will go out and leap like calves of the stall.
verses.arminianNotes:
“But to you who fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings.” Arminian readers note the contrast between judgment and healing.

Many Christians hear an anticipation of Christ (cf. Luke 1:78), a reading held with care.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hear hope for those who fear God, and many share the Christological reading.

Shared ground: both traditions rejoice in the image of joy, with the faithful going out “like calves of the stall.”

verses.text: You shall tread down the wicked; for they will be ashes under the soles of your feet in the day that I make,” says the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You shall tread down the wicked; for they will be ashes under the soles of your feet in the day that I make.” Arminian readers note the reversal: the oppressed are vindicated.

The day belongs to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s justice bringing final vindication.

Shared ground: both traditions read the image as poetry about God’s victory over evil, not as a call for personal revenge.

verses.text: “Remember the law of Moses my servant, which I commanded to him in Horeb for all Israel, even statutes and ordinances.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Remember the law of Moses my servant, which I commanded to him in Horeb for all Israel.” Arminian readers note the call to remember God’s word.

The prophetic books close by pointing back to Moses.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the law as the standard by which God’s people live while awaiting his coming.

Shared ground: both traditions note that Moses and Elijah appear together at the transfiguration (Matt 17:3), named without merging the passages.

verses.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the LORD comes.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the LORD comes.” Arminian readers note the promise of a forerunner.

Jesus identifies John the Baptist with this Elijah (Matt 11:14; 17:11–13).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hear the Gospels’ application, while noting that John denies being Elijah in person (John 1:21).

Shared ground: both traditions name these passages without merging them, and both read the phrase “great and terrible day” with Joel 2:31.

verses.text: He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.” Arminian readers note the promise of reconciliation.

Luke 1:17 applies these words to John.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the forerunner’s work as preparing a people for the Lord.

Shared ground: both traditions read the closing warning soberly and agree that the book ends with a call to repentance and the hope of restored relationships.
